title: Distributed Trotterization with optimal time-scaling entanglement cost
authors: Tianfeng Feng, Jinzhao Sun, Yunlong Xiao, Qi Zhao
abstract: Distributed architectures extend quantum simulation of many-body dynamics beyond the reach of any single processor, with shared entanglement mediating interactions between spatially separated devices. Conventional implementations rely on quantum teleportation, which provides a universal realization of nonlocal operations but incurs a fixed entanglement cost per gate, irrespective of its strength. This becomes increasingly inefficient in product formula simulation, where higher accuracy requires ever more numerous, yet progressively weaker, nonlocal rotations, causing the entanglement cost to diverge in the high-accuracy limit. Here we introduce a simple repeat-until-success protocol that makes entanglement consumption adaptive to interaction strength. Incorporating this primitive into distributed product formulas yields a total entanglement cost that scales linearly with evolution time and remains independent of Trotter error. A matching lower bound from quantum communication complexity proves this time scaling to be optimal, establishing a resource-efficient foundation for high-accuracy quantum simulation across networked processors.
summary: This paper introduces an adaptive Repeat-Until-Success (RUS) protocol to simulate quantum dynamics across multiple processors. It demonstrates that this protocol allows the total entanglement cost to scale only linearly with simulation time, independent of the required accuracy. This linear scaling is proven to be optimal, establishing a resource-efficient foundation for high-fidelity quantum simulation on distributed hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the resource-efficient simulation of many-body dynamics on distributed quantum processors, specifically minimizing the entanglement cost associated with nonlocal operations.
main_result: By using a Repeat-Until-Success (RUS) protocol, the total entanglement cost for high-accuracy simulation scales only linearly with the evolution time ($O(t)$), which is proven to be optimal.
method: The authors compare the entanglement cost scaling of the proposed adaptive RUS protocol against conventional teleportation methods within the framework of product formula Trotterization.
model_or_system: The model is the distributed quantum simulation of a many-body system governed by a Hamiltonian $H = H_A + H_B + H_{AB}$, where interactions occur between spatially separated subsystems A and B.
key_observables: Entanglement Cost (measured in ebits), Total Entanglement Cost scaling ($O(t)$ vs. superlinear/divergent), and Simulation Error ($\epsilon$).
important_parameters: Evolution Time ($t$), Target Error ($\epsilon$), Trotterization Order ($q$), and Interaction Strengths ($J_x$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of the RUS protocol and relies on matching lower bounds from quantum communication complexity to establish optimality.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the distributed simulation setup, the RUS protocol mechanism, and the comparative scaling of entanglement costs showing $C_{	ext{RUS}}$ remaining linear while $C_{	ext{TEL}}$ diverges as accuracy increases.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of resource-intensive nonlocal gates in distributed simulation. It then introduces and analyzes the RUS protocol, deriving its expected entanglement cost. Finally, it compares this cost scaling against standard teleportation methods, proving the linear scaling is optimal.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the resource scaling bottleneck in large-scale quantum simulation, providing a theoretically optimal resource estimate for networked quantum processors.
